title: NRI Property Sales Get Easier From October as India Drops TAN Requirement for Buyers
excerpt: Budget 2026 changes let resident buyers use PAN-based challans for TDS when purchasing property from NRIs, eliminating a major compliance hurdle.
body:
• From October 1, 2026, resident buyers purchasing property from NRIs can deduct and deposit TDS using a PAN-based challan instead of obtaining a separate TAN.
  • The change eliminates a major compliance barrier that previously delayed NRI property transactions and discouraged resident buyers.
  • NRI sellers still face TDS rates of up to 12.5% plus surcharge on long-term capital gains unless they obtain a Lower TDS Certificate (Form 13).
  • FEMA repatriation rules require Form 15CA, Form 15CB and Form A2 filings to transfer sale proceeds abroad.

Non-Resident Indians selling property in India will benefit from simplified compliance starting October 1, 2026, after the Union Budget proposed eliminating the Tax Deduction Account Number (TAN) requirement for resident buyers in NRI property transactions.

What Changes

Under current rules, when the seller of immovable property is a non-resident, the buyer must obtain a TAN to deduct tax at source under Section 195 of the Income Tax Act. This requirement has long been a friction point — most Indian buyers are unfamiliar with TAN procedures and find the added compliance burden discouraging, especially for a single transaction.

The Budget 2026 amendment allows resident buyers to deduct and deposit TDS through a PAN-based challan instead. "TDS on the sale of immovable property by a non-resident is proposed to be deducted and deposited through resident buyer's PAN-based challan instead of requiring TAN," Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said in her Budget speech, as reported by The Hindu Business Line.

"The property must have updated documentation with proper title deeds, encumbrance certificate, tax receipt, approved plan, and other necessary documents. Lack of proper documentation might pose problems when carrying out the transactions."

— E. Lakshminarayana Reddy, Founder and CEO, EARA Group

Common Pitfalls NRIs Should Avoid

Even with the simplified TAN process, NRI property transactions remain complex. According to Magicbricks, the most common mistakes include assuming the standard 1% TDS rate applies (NRI transactions require withholding under Section 195 at higher rates), failing to obtain a Lower TDS Certificate through Form 13, and making inaccurate capital gains calculations by omitting improvement costs and inflation adjustments.

Without a Lower TDS Certificate, buyers may be required to deduct up to 14.95% from the total sale price — not just the capital gains — potentially locking up a significant portion of the sale proceeds in the tax system until the seller files for a refund.

Repatriation: The Three-Form Process

NRIs looking to transfer sale proceeds abroad must navigate FEMA's compliance requirements, which involve three separate filings: Form 15CB (a mandatory certificate from a Chartered Accountant verifying the remittance), Form 15CA (the remitter's declaration filed on the tax portal), and Form A2 (the FEMA-specific application submitted to the bank under Code S0021).

Annuity payouts and property sale proceeds must be credited to an NRO account before remittance. NRE account holders can repatriate freely, while NRO account holders face a $1 million annual limit with required documentation.

Bottom Line for NRIs

The October 2026 deadline makes this an actionable window for NRIs considering property transactions. Those planning to sell should ensure documentation is current, apply for a Lower TDS Certificate early, and consult a qualified Chartered Accountant familiar with FEMA compliance to avoid delays and penalties of up to three times the transaction value.
nri_angle: NRIs selling property in India will face significantly less red tape from October 2026 as the TAN requirement is dropped for resident buyers.
author: Diaspora Desk
